podcast.body: This song was recorded by Jerry Lee Lewis almost as a joke during his first solo session for Sun Records, having also played it on his audition tape. It was a bit of a disappointment to him because his father, Elmo Lewis, who had given up his own piano playing ambition, wasn't impressed, finding it bittersweet to see his son achieve what he couldn't. The conventional narrative credits Ralph Mooney with writing it in 1949, with a demo by Windstewet in 1954, and the first release by Marilyn Kay before Ray Price's version became the biggest country hit of 1956, changing honky-tonk music with its four-notes-in-a-bar bass line. "Crazy Arms would always be a bit of a disappointment to Jerry Lee, not because it wasn't a massive hit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.body: Toward the end of the Million Dollar Quartet jam session, when Elvis Presley was in the control room, Jerry Lee Lewis took over completely, playing by himself and singing this song, showcasing his solo talents. "The last few songs in the jam session are essentially Lewis playing by himself, singing crazy arms, and Jean Ortee's, you're the only star in my blue heaven, and playing the old Jelly Roll Morton piano piece, Black Bottom Stomp."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
